content: At baseline, tuberculosis (TB) was identified in some participants. For the study visit at 48 weeks, a pre-defined window of ±6 weeks was allowed, and follow-up time was censored at 54 weeks. Cox regression analysis was employed to estimate the hazard ratio for time to TB endpoint when comparing levofloxacin (Lfx) to placebo, accounting for household clustering and adjusting for site and age group. Safety analyses included all randomized participants who received at least one dose of the study drug, with comparisons made for the time to the first adverse event between treatment arms. Additionally, individual patient data (IPD) and Bayesian analyses were conducted, including data from the TB-CHAMP and V-QUIN studies. In the V-QUIN study, the placebo group was expected to have a 3% risk of developing TB during the follow-up period, with a 70% reduction in TB incidence anticipated in the Lfx treatment group based on prior isoniazid efficacy estimates for drug-susceptible TB. The study design accounted for clustering at the district and household levels, with a power of 80% and a significance level of 0.05. Statistical analyses followed a pre-specified plan, with group assignments blinded until analyses were complete. The primary analysis included the intention-to-treat (ITT) population, while secondary outcomes (e.g., bacteriologically confirmed or clinically probable TB and all-cause mortality) were also analyzed using ITT. The per-protocol population included participants who completed at least 80% of their assigned treatment. The modified ITT (mITT) population excluded contacts of patients with rifampicin-susceptible TB and those who did not initiate therapy. An interim safety analysis assessed the rate of grade 3 and 4 adverse events after 600 participants completed six months of therapy. A secondary Bayesian analysis evaluated the incidence of confirmed or probable TB at 54 weeks. Incidence rate ratios and 95% confidence intervals were estimated using a marginal Poisson regression model with generalized estimating equations. Complete case analysis was performed for both primary and secondary outcomes. The TB-CHAMP trial focused on children exposed to multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) in household settings. Of the 922 child participants enrolled from 497 households, 453 were assigned to Lfx, and 469 to placebo. The mITT population included 451 and 465 participants in the Lfx and placebo groups, respectively. Participants were excluded from the per-protocol population for reasons such as receiving incorrect treatment, non-adherence, or missing adherence data. Safety outcomes showed that Lfx was well-tolerated, with only six children discontinuing treatment due to adverse events compared to one in the placebo group. The incidence of TB endpoints was lower than expected, and a high proportion of children were screened out due to presumptive TB. IGRA positivity rates were also lower than anticipated. The V-QUIN trial demonstrated a 45% reduction in microbiologically confirmed TB incidence at 30 months with Lfx. However, the primary analysis had broad confidence intervals, which included the null, indicating no statistical significance. Grade 3–4 adverse events were rare, with no differences observed between groups. No acquired drug resistance to Lfx was detected. A sub-study revealed persistent reductions in microbiome diversity six months post-therapy, with increased nasal carriage of fluoroquinolone-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. A systematic review of fluoroquinolone (FQ)-based TB preventive treatment (TPT) for MDR-TB contacts found no randomized controlled trials addressing efficacy. Observational studies suggested that FQ-based TPT is safe, with no grade 3, 4, or serious adverse events reported. Completion rates and acceptability were high, though mild or moderate adverse events were observed in children and adolescents. Cost-effectiveness modeling indicated that targeting high-risk groups, such as children under 5 or those under 15 with HIV, was the most cost-effective strategy. Providing TPT to all children under 15 had the greatest impact on reducing deaths and life-years lost. In conclusion, while FQ-based TPT appears safe and acceptable, high-quality evidence on its efficacy for preventing MDR-TB disease is lacking. Further research is needed to establish its effectiveness in reducing TB incidence among contacts of MDR-TB patients.
